132. Since man is such as not to be content to be led by the Lord, but desires also to be guided by himself and the—

---

used that word which most adequately exhibits the *sense*: for it is in reference to woman in her character as the *wife* of man, that the original adverts to the derivation of her name. On this account, then, our author, after having in the 22nd verse translated the word [woman/wife] <note>original Hebrew: "ishah"</note>—woman <note>original Latin: "mulier"</note>, as most agreeable to the sense in that place, translates it in this verse wife <note>original Latin: "uxor"</note>—as most expressive of the meaning here. In the following verse—the 24th—the translators of the authorized version of the Bible have also made the same change of terms: as we cannot say in English "a man shall cleave to his *woman*," they have there introduced the term "wife" as their translation of [woman/wife] <note>original Hebrew: "ishah"</note>. The difficulty arises from this circumstance. The Hebrew word [woman/wife] <note>original Hebrew: "ishah"</note>, like the French word *femme*, means both a *woman*, in general, and a *wife*, in particular; and therefore in languages like the English, which appropriate a separate word to express each of those ideas, it must be translated either by the one term or the other, according to the sense, as determined by the context.

From this statement it will also be seen, that when the author says below, n. 151, that the selfhood "is called a *woman*, and afterwards a *wife*," he does not mean that the words in the Hebrew are different, but that different words are used by him, because the *idea* attached to the same Hebrew word is different in different places.

\* It is necessary to explain why the Latin word [male man] <note>original: "vir"</note> is here and in other places added in brackets after the word "man."

In the three ancient languages, the Hebrew, the Greek, and the Latin, there are two words to denote man; one of these words, which in Hebrew is [human] <note>original: "adam"</note>, in Greek, [human] <note>original: "anthropos"</note>, and in Latin, [human] <note>original: "homo"</note>, denoting a human being in general, without any reference to sex; and the other, which in Hebrew is [male] <note>original: "ish"</note>, in Greek, [male] <note>original: "aner"</note>, and in Latin, [male] <note>original: "vir"</note>, denoting a *male* man only. But as the English affords but the single word "man," by which to translate the twofold expressions of the ancient languages; and as, on account of the distinctness of the ideas in the spiritual sense, it is necessary to indicate, by some means, what expression is used in the author's Latin, and in the passages of the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures which he translates, therefore throughout this work, when the word in the Latin is [human] <note>original: "homo"</note>, answering to the Greek [human] <note>original: "anthropos"</note> and the Hebrew [human] <note>original: "adam"</note>, the English word "man" is given by itself; but when the word in the Latin is [male] <note>original: "vir"</note>, answering to the Greek [male] <note>original: "aner"</note> and the Hebrew [male] <note>original: "ish"</note>, the Latin word [male] <note>original: "vir"</note> is added, as above.

### THE INTERNAL SENSE.

137. THE first three chapters of Genesis treat in general of the <term>Most Ancient Church</term> <note>This refers to the very first spiritual era of humanity, which existed in a state of direct, heart-centered perception of divine truth.</note> which is called *Man*, from its beginning to its end, when it perished : the preceding part of this chapter treated of its most flourishing state, when it was a <term>celestial man</term> <note>A state of human development where love for the Lord is the primary motivation for every thought and action.</note> ; the present, of those who inclined to <term>selfhood</term> and of their posterity.

138. Verse 18. *And Jehovah God said, It is not good that the man should be alone ; I will make him a help as with him.* By *alone* is signified, that he was not content to be led by the Lord, but desired to be so from self and the world. By *a help as with him*, is signified the <term>selfhood</term>, which is subsequently called *a rib built into a woman*.

139. In ancient times those were said to dwell alone who were under the Lord’s guidance as celestial men, because such were no longer infested by evils, or evil spirits. This was also represented in the Jewish Church by their *dwelling alone* when they had driven out the nations. On this account it is frequently said of the Lord’s Church in the Word, that she is *alone*, as in Jeremiah : “Arise, get you up to the quiet nation that dwelleth confidently, saith the Lord, which hath neither gates nor bars, they *dwell alone*,” (xlix. 31.) In the prophecy of Moses : “*Israel hath dwelt confidently alone*,” (Deut. xxxiii. 28.) And still more clearly in the prophecy of Balaam : “*Lo, the people dwelleth alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations*,” (Numb. xxiii. 9 ;) where nations signify evils. This posterity of the <term>Most Ancient Church</term> was not disposed to *dwell alone*, that is, to be a celestial man, or to be led by the Lord as a celestial man, but to live amongst the nations like the Jewish Church. In consequence of this inclination, it is said, *it is not good that the*

140. That by a *help as with him* the <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "proprium"; refers to the Latin concept of what is one's own, the "ego" or sense of self that feels independent from God.</note> is signified, is evident both from the nature of the <term>selfhood</term>, and from what follows. As, however, the man of the church, who is here treated of, was well disposed, a <term>selfhood</term> was granted to him, but of such a kind that it appeared like his own, wherefore it is said to be a *help as with him*.

141. Innumerable circumstances might be related about the <term>selfhood</term>, in describing its nature and influence with the corporeal and worldly man, with the spiritual man, and with the celestial man. The <term>selfhood</term>, with the corporeal and worldly man, is his all; he knows nothing else but the <term>selfhood</term>, and imagines, as was said above, that if he were to lose his <term>selfhood</term> he should perish. With the spiritual man also the <term>selfhood</term> has a similar appearance; for, although he knows that the Lord is the life of all, and gives wisdom and understanding, and consequently the power to think and to act, yet this knowledge is rather the profession of his lips than the belief of his heart. But the <term>celestial man</term> <note>A person in the highest state of spiritual development, who acts from a heart full of love for God rather than just from a sense of duty or intellect.</note> acknowledges that the Lord is the life of all, and gives the power to think and to act, because he perceives that it is really so. He never desires a <term>selfhood</term>; but although he does not, still a <term>selfhood</term> is given him by the Lord, which is conjoined with every perception of the good and the true, and with all felicity. The angels are in such a <term>selfhood</term>, and thence in the utmost peace and tranquillity; for in their <term>selfhood</term> are contained the things which are of the Lord, who governs their <term>selfhood</term>, or them by means of their <term>selfhood</term>. This <term>selfhood</term> is the very essence of all that is celestial, whilst that of the corporeal man is <term>infernal</term> <note>pertaining to hell or a state of spiritual separation from the Divine</note> :—but, more will be said hereafter on the subject of the <term>selfhood</term>.

To bring them to the man to see what he would call them, is to enable him to know their quality, and his giving them names, signifies that he knew it. But, notwithstanding he knew with what quality the affections of the good and the knowledges of the true were endowed by the Lord, still he inclined to <term>selfhood</term>, which is expressed in the same terms as before, that *there was not found a help as with him*.

143. The idea that human affections and similar traits are represented by animals may seem strange today. However, the people of that ancient period viewed everything through a celestial lens. In the <note>In Swedenborg’s theology, the "world of spirits" is an intermediate state where internal thoughts and feelings are visibly manifested as representative objects or animals.</note> world of spirits, such things are actually represented by *animals*—specifically by animals that match the character of the affection. Therefore, when animals were mentioned in the Word, these specific qualities were understood. The entire prophetic Word is filled with these representative expressions. Because of this, anyone who does not know the specific significance of each *beast* cannot possibly understand the <term>internal sense</term> <note>The "internal sense" refers to the deeper spiritual meaning hidden beneath the literal text of the Bible.</note> of the Scriptures. As previously noted, *beasts* are categorized into two kinds: evil or harmful ones, and good or harmless ones. The *good* signify positive affections, such as sheep, lambs, and doves. Since the text here describes the celestial or <term>celestial-spiritual man</term> <note>A "celestial-spiritual man" is someone whose life is governed by a combination of heavenly love and spiritual truth.</note>, it is these good animals that are meant. We have already shown from other parts of the Word (in sections 45 and 46) that beasts generally signify affections, so there is no need for further proof here.

144. To *call by name* signifies knowing the quality or character of a thing. This is because the ancients understood a *name* to be nothing other than the "essence" of a thing; thus, to *see and call by name* meant to perceive its true nature. This is why they gave *names* to their sons and daughters based on what they represented. Every *name* had a specific meaning, allowing people to know a person's origin and character. This will be explored later in this work, by the Lord’s divine mercy, when we discuss the twelve sons of <note>original: "Jacob"; the biblical patriarch whose sons became the twelve tribes of Israel.</note> Jacob. Since *names* revealed the "whence and what" of a person, *calling by name* was simply their way of describing the act of understanding someone’s nature. This was a common way of speaking for them, though it may surprise those unfamiliar with ancient customs.

145. Throughout the Word, *name* signifies the essence of a thing, and *seeing and calling by name* means knowing its quality. This is seen in <note>original: "Esaias"; the prophet Isaiah.</note> Isaiah:

This signifies acquiring a new nature, as is clear from the surrounding verses. Again:

146. From what has been stated, the connection of these meanings can be seen. In verse 18 it is said, *It is not good that the man should be alone, I will make him a help as with him*; shortly after, *beasts* and *birds* are mentioned—which had already been mentioned earlier in the text—and then it is immediately repeated that *for the man there was not found a help as with him*. For those who are of such a nature that they desire a <term>selfhood</term> begin to look down upon the things of the Lord, no matter how clearly those truths are shown or proven to them.

147. *And Jehovah God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in the place thereof.* By a *rib*, which is a bone of the chest, is meant man's <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "proprium"</note>, in which there is very little spiritual life, and yet it is a <term>selfhood</term> that is very dear to him. By *flesh in the place of the rib*, is meant a <term>selfhood</term> that has been given life by the Lord. By a *deep sleep* is meant that state he was led into so that he might seem to himself to possess a <term>selfhood</term> of his own. This state is compared to *sleep* because, while in it, a person does not know any differently than that he lives, thinks, speaks, and acts entirely from himself. However, when he begins to realize that this is a false perception, he is then roused, as if from *sleep*, and becomes awake.

148. The reason why man's <term>selfhood</term>, represented by a bone of the chest and held so dear, is called a *rib*, is because the chest, among the people of the <term>Most Ancient Church</term> <note>The Most Ancient Church refers to the earliest era of humanity, who were said to perceive spiritual truths directly through their feelings and perceptions.</note>, signified charity, as it contains both the heart and the lungs. Bones signified the lesser or "viler" things because they have the very minimum of life in them, while *flesh* represented things that possessed true life. The reasoning behind these meanings is one of the deepest <term>mysteries</term> <note>original Latin: "arcana"</note> known to the people of the Most Ancient Church, about which more will be said, by the Lord’s divine mercy, in the pages to follow.

"...your bones shall flourish like an herb," (Isaiah 66:14). In David: "All my bones shall say, Jehovah, who is like unto thee?" (Psalm 35:10). This is still more evident from Ezekiel, where he speaks of bones receiving *flesh*, and having breath put into them: "The hand of Jehovah—hath sent me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones, and he said to me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of Jehovah; thus saith the Lord Jehovah to these *bones*; behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live: and I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up *flesh* upon you, and cover you with skin, and I will put breath in you, and ye shall live, and ye shall know that I am Jehovah," (Ezekiel 37:1, 4—6).

Man's <term>selfhood</term> <note>original Latin: *proprium*; a technical term in this theology referring to the human ego or the sense of having a life and identity independent from God</note>, when viewed from heaven, appears altogether like something bony, inanimate, and thoroughly deformed, and is consequently, in itself, dead; but when given life by the Lord, it looks like a *fleshy substance*. Man's <term>selfhood</term> is, indeed, a mere dead nothing, although to him it seems so real and important—even as his very all. Whatever lives in him is from the life of the Lord, and if this were removed, he would fall down dead like a stone: for man is only an organ receptive of life, and just as the quality of the organ varies, so does the feeling of that life. The Lord alone has <term>true selfhood</term>; from His own <term>selfhood</term> He redeemed man, and from His own <term>selfhood</term> He saves man. The Lord's <term>selfhood</term> is life itself, and from His <term>selfhood</term>, man's <term>selfhood</term>—which in itself is dead—is made alive. The Lord's <term>selfhood</term> is also signified by the Lord's words in Luke: "A spirit hath not *flesh and bones as ye see me have*," (Luke 24:39); and likewise by the instruction that a *bone of the paschal lamb should not be broken* (Exodus 12:46).

150. The state of man when he is in his <term>selfhood</term>, or when he supposes his life to be self-derived, is compared to *deep sleep*. Indeed, by the ancient people, it was called *deep sleep*, and in the Word it is said of such people that *they have poured out upon them the spirit of deep sleep, and that they sleep the sleep*. Man's <term>selfhood</term> is in itself dead, and no one has any life from himself. This is shown so clearly in the world of spirits <note>a transitional state after death where spirits are prepared for heaven or hell</note> that evil spirits, who love nothing but their own <term>selfhood</term> and obstinately insist that they live from themselves, are eventually convinced by direct experience and forced to confess that they do not live from themselves. It has been especially permitted me, now for several years, to become acquainted with the human <term>selfhood</term>, and it has been granted to me to perceive clearly that I could think nothing from myself, but that every idea of thought entered by <term>influx</term> <note>the flow of spiritual life or thought from God through the spiritual world into the individual mind</note>, and sometimes I perceived how and from where this <term>influx</term> entered. Therefore, the person who supposes that he lives from himself is in a state of falsehood, and consequently claims for himself everything evil and false—which he would never do if he believed the real truth of the matter.

Verse 22. *And the rib which Jehovah God had taken from the man, he built into a woman, and brought her to the man.* By "to *build*" is signified the raising up of that which has fallen; by the "rib," the <term>unvivified selfhood</term> <note>original Latin: *proprium*; refers to the human ego or the sense of having a life and identity independent from God. "Unvivified" means it has not yet been given spiritual life</note>; by a "woman," the <term>selfhood</term> given life by the Lord; by "he brought her to the man," it is signified that this <term>selfhood</term> was granted to him. The descendants of this church did not wish, like their ancestors, to be a "celestial man" <note>a person in perfect, direct harmony with the Divine</note>, but desired to be under their own self-guidance; and, as they were thus inclining toward their own <term>selfhood</term>, it was granted to them—yet it was a <term>selfhood</term> still given life by the Lord, and therefore called a *woman*, and afterwards a *wife*.

152. It requires but little attention for anyone to discern that a woman was not literally formed out of the rib of a man, and that deeper <term>inner secrets</term> <note>original Latin: *arcana*; hidden spiritual truths within the literal words of scripture</note> are implied here than any person has heretofore been aware of. It must be plain also, that by the "woman" is signified the <term>selfhood</term>, from the fact that it was the woman who was deceived; for nothing ever deceives man except his own <term>selfhood</term>, or, what is the same thing, the love of self and of the world.

153. *The rib is said to be built into a woman*, but it is not stated that the woman was "created," or "formed," or "made," as was the case previously when the text treated of regeneration <note>the process of being spiritually reborn</note>. The reason it is said to be *built* is because to "build" is to raise up that which is fallen. In this sense, the term is applied in the Word <note>the Bible</note>, where to *build* is predicted of evils; to "raise up" is predicted of falsities; and to *renew* is predicted of both; as in Isaiah: 
> “They shall *build* the wastes of eternity, they shall raise up the ancient desolations, and they shall *renew* the waste cities, the desolations of many generations,” (61:4). 

"Wastes" in this and other passages signify evils; "desolations" signify falsities; "to *build*" is applied to the former, and "to raise up" to the latter, and this distinction is carefully observed in other places by the prophets, as where it is said in Jeremiah: 
> “Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel,” (31:4).

154. Thus, any person to whom the things of their own <term>selfhood</term> are visibly shown is struck with horror and wishes to flee from himself as if from a devil. When, however, the things of the <term>selfhood</term> of man are given life by the Lord, they assume a beautiful and graceful form, varying according to the type of life to which the Lord's celestial principle can be joined. ## ON THE RESURRECTION OF MAN FROM THE DEAD, AND HIS ENTRANCE INTO ETERNAL LIFE.

168. *Being permitted to describe in a series the way in which man passes from the life of the body into the life of eternity, so that I might understand the process by which he is <term>resuscitated</term> <note>original: "resuscitetur"; here meaning the awakening or "rising again" of the spirit immediately after the death of the physical body</note>, I was, as has been stated, instructed not by hearing words, but by direct sensory experience.*

169. *I was reduced into a state of insensibility in my physical senses, much like the state of dying persons; however, my interior life remained fully intact, along with the power of thought. This was done so that I might perceive and remember what happens to those who die and are awakened. I was left with just enough breathing to sustain life, and later with <term>tacit respiration</term> <note>A form of internal or "silent" breathing that does not rely on the physical lungs, said to be the manner in which spirits and angels breathe</note>.*

170. *<term>Celestial angels</term> <note>In this system, the "celestial" are the highest order of angels, defined by their intense love and connection to the heart and the "will"</note> came and occupied the region of the heart, so that in regard to my heart, I seemed united with them. Eventually, almost nothing was left to me except thought and the perception resulting from it; and I remained in this state for several hours.*

171. *In this way, I was removed from communication with spirits in the <term>world of spirits</term> <note>The intermediate realm where souls go immediately after death before eventually moving to heaven or hell</note>, who believed that I had passed away from the life of the body.*

172. *In addition to the celestial angels who occupied the region of the heart, there were also two angels sitting at my head. It was given to me to perceive that this is the case for every person who dies.*

173. *The angels who sat at my head were perfectly silent, communicating their thoughts only through their faces. I could perceive that another face was, as it were, superimposed upon mine—or rather two faces, because there were two angels. When the angels perceive that their faces are received by the dying person, they know that the person has died.*

174. *After they recognized their faces in mine, they induced certain changes around the region of the mouth and communicated their thoughts in that way. It is the custom for celestial angels to speak through the province of the mouth; and I was permitted to perceive this <term>cogitative speech</term> <note>Communication consisting of pure thought and intent rather than audible words</note>.*

175. *I perceived an aromatic odor, like that of an embalmed corpse. When the celestial angels are present, the smell of a dead body is perceived as a pleasant fragrance; when evil spirits recognize this scent, they are prevented from approaching the person.*

176. *In the meantime, I perceived that the region of my heart was kept closely united with the celestial angels, which was also evident from my pulse.*

177. *It was suggested to me that the angels keep the man engaged in the pious and holy thoughts he held at the moment of death. It was also shared that those who die usually think about eternal life, and only rarely about salvation or happiness; therefore, the angels keep their focus specifically on the thought of eternal life.*

## THE INTERNAL SENSE.

194. VERSE 1. *And the serpent was more subtle than any wild beast of the field which Jehovah God had made; and he said to the woman, Hath not God, moreover, said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?* By the serpent is here meant the sensual principle <note>The "sensual principle" refers to the lowest part of the human mind which perceives the world through the five senses and often doubts what it cannot see or touch.</note> of man, when depended upon; by the wild beast of the field, as before, every affection of the external man, by the woman, <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "proprium"; this refers to the human ego or the sense of "self" that feels independent from God.</note>; by the serpent’s saying, *Hath not God, moreover, said, Ye shall not eat of every tree?* that they began to doubt. This is said of the third generation of the Most Ancient Church <note>The "Most Ancient Church" is a term used to describe the first state of humanity, which lived in a direct, intuitive relationship with the Divine before the fall.</note>, which began to disbelieve such revelations as they could not see, and perceive the evidence of: their first state is described in this and the subsequent verse, as a state of doubt.

195. The most ancient people did not compare all things in man to beasts and birds, but they so denominated them; and this their customary manner of speaking remained even in the Ancient Church after the flood, and was preserved amongst the prophets. The sensual things in man they called *serpents*, because as *serpents* live close to the earth, so sensual things are closely connected with the body. Hence also reasonings concerning the mysteries of faith, founded on the evidence of the senses, were spoken of by them as the *poison of a serpent*, and the reasoners themselves as *serpents*; and because such reasoners argue much from sensual or visible things, which are terrestrial, corporeal, mundane and natural, therefore the *serpent was said to be more subtle than any wild beast of the field*. It is likewise said by David, speaking of those who seduce man by reasonings, 
> "They have sharpened their tongue like a *serpent*; the poison of the *asp* is under their lips," (Psalm cxl. 3.) 
And again: 
> "They are estranged from the womb—speaking a lie. Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: like the deaf poisonous *asp* that stoppeth her ear, that she may not hear the voice of charmers, the companionship of the wise companion <note>original: "incantantis sapienter"; referring to one who charms or teaches with wisdom.</note>," (Psalm lviii. 3—6.) 
Reasonings are here called the *poison of a serpent*, which induce an unwillingness to hear the wise, or the voice of the wise; hence it became a proverb amongst the ancients, that *the serpent stoppeth the ear*. It is said in Amos,

196. In ancient times, those were called *serpents* who had more confidence in sensual things than in revealed truth. Have not animals a body, senses, and something analogous to reason? and yet it is asserted that although these must all perish the spirit of man is immortal: thus they deny the existence of the spirit. ### 200.
The reason why the *tree of knowledge* is here spoken of as being in the *midst of the garden*, although previously (Genesis 2:9,) the *tree of lives* was said to be in the *midst of the garden*, and not the *tree of knowledge*, is because the *midst of the garden* signifies the inmost <note>The "inmost" refers to the deepest, most central part of a person's soul or consciousness.</note>; and the inmost <insert>principle</insert> of the <term>celestial man</term> <note>A "celestial man" is one who acts purely from love and internal perception rather than external rules or logic.</note>, or the Most Ancient Church, was the *tree of lives*, which is love and the faith derived from it; whereas with this man, who may be called a celestial-spiritual man, or with this descendant, faith was the *midst of the garden*, or the inmost. It is impossible more fully to describe the nature of the men who lived in that most ancient time, because in the present day it is utterly unknown, their disposition being altogether different from our own. For the purpose, however, of conveying some faint idea of their disposition, it may be mentioned that they knew what was true from what was good, or what belongs to faith from love. But, when that generation passed away, another succeeded of a totally different nature, for instead of discerning the true from the good, or what was of faith from love, they acquired the knowledge of what is good by means of the true, and what is of love from the knowledges of faith, and with many amongst them mere knowledge alone was the <gloss>thing desired</gloss> <note>original Latin: "desideratum"</note>. Such was the change made after the flood to prevent the destruction of the world.

# GENESIS. [CHAP. iii.

[pro]prium <note>Continuing from the previous page: this refers to the human "selfhood" or ego.</note>, and was unwilling to believe what was revealed, unless confirmed by the evidence of the senses and by science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "scientifics"—knowledge gained through the physical senses rather than spiritual perception.</note>.

209. The expressions here employed, as that *the tree was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable for giving intelligence*, are such as were adapted to the genius of those who lived in that most ancient time, having especial reference to the will, because their evils originated in the will. Where the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Sacred Scripture or Divine Revelation.</note> treats of the people who lived after the flood, such expressions are adopted as are not thus applicable to the will, but to the understanding; for the most ancient people derived the true from the good, whilst those who lived after the flood acquired the good by means of the true.

210. The nature of the <term>proprium</term> <note>A Latin term for "that which is one's own." It describes the human sense of self that feels independent of the Divine; it is the root of pride and self-reliance.</note> may be understood from the fact of every evil and false in man originating in the love of self and the world, whereby men are inclined to believe in self, and not in the Lord or the Word, and to suppose that what they cannot acquire sensually and scientifically has no existence. Hence they become altogether evil and false, and thus see all things so perversely as to regard evil as good, and good as evil; falses as truths, and truths as falses; realities as nothing, and nothing as every thing. They call hatred love, darkness light, death life, and *vice versa* <note>original: "vice versa," meaning "the other way around."</note>, and are denominated in the Word, *the lame and the blind*. This then is the <term>proprium</term> of man, which is, in itself, infernal and accursed.

211. Verse 7. *And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked.* Their eyes being opened, signifies their knowing and acknowledging, in consequence of an internal dictate <note>An inner awareness or spiritual intuition.</note>, themselves to be naked, that is, no longer in innocence, as before, but in evil.

212. By *having the eyes opened* is signified an interior dictate, as is evident from similar expressions in the Word; as from what Balaam says of himself, who, in consequence of having visions, calls himself *the man whose eyes were opened* (Numb. xxiv. 3.) And from Jonathan, who, when he tasted of the honey-comb, and had a dictate from within that it was evil, said that his *eyes saw so as to be enlightened* so that he saw what he knew not, (1 Sam. xiv. 29.) Besides, in the Word, *the eyes* are often used to denote the understanding, and thus an interior impression thence received; as in David: "Lighten mine *eyes*, lest I should sleep the death," (Psalm xiii. 3;) where *eyes* denote the understanding. So in Ezekiel, speaking of those who are not willing to understand, "who have *eyes to see, and see not*," (xii. 2.) In Isaiah: "Shut their *eyes*, lest they should see with their *eyes*," (vi. 10,) for blind them lest they should understand. So Moses says to the people, "Jehovah hath not given you a heart to know, and *eyes to see*, and ears to hear," (Deut. xxix. 4;) where heart is put for the will, and *eyes* for the [understanding].

*“...and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you,”* (Isaiah lix. 2;) and here, they hid themselves from the face of Jehovah, because they were naked. <note>In this context, being "naked" refers to the loss of spiritual innocence and the realization of one's own selfish nature.</note>

224. Mercy, peace, and every good—otherwise called ***the faces of Jehovah*** <note>original: "facies Jehovae". In Hebrew thought, the "face" represents the presence, favor, and inner character of a person.</note>—are the source of the <term>internal dictate</term> <note>An inner prompting or spiritual "gut feeling" regarding truth.</note> experienced by those who possess <term>perception</term>. These same qualities affect those who have <term>conscience</term>, though in a different way. They always operate with mercy, yet they are received differently depending on a person's spiritual state. The state of this "man"—meaning the descendants of the <term>Most Ancient Church</term> <note>The earliest, most spiritually pure state of humanity described in the Bible.</note>—was still good in a <term>natural degree</term> <note>Goodness based on external behavior and feelings rather than deep spiritual wisdom.</note>. 225. ***The midst of the tree of the garden*** signifies natural good, which contains a degree of <term>perception</term> (here called a **tree**). Good is not truly good unless its innermost core is celestial; it is from or through this core that the Lord provides perception. This innermost principle is here called **the midst**, a term used similarly elsewhere in the <term>Word</term> <note>The Holy Scriptures.</note>.

In the Word, it is common for a person to be asked where they are or what they are doing, even though the Lord already knows everything about them. The reason for this inquiry is so that the person might acknowledge and confess their own state.

227. Because the origin of perception, internal dictate, and conscience is currently completely unknown, I am permitted to share something on the subject. It is a fundamental truth that the Lord governs man by means of spirits and angels. When evil spirits begin to take control, angels work to turn away the resulting evils and falsehoods, leading to a struggle. It is this very combat that a person feels through perception, internal dictates, impressions, or conscience. Through these experiences—as well as through spiritual trials—a person could clearly know that spirits and angels are with them, if they were not so focused on bodily concerns that they refused to believe anything said about the spiritual world. Such people, even if they felt these internal struggles hundreds of times, would still claim they were merely imaginary or the result of a disordered mind. 233. To explore the mysteries of faith by <term>scientifics</term> <note>In this context, "scientifics" refers to factual knowledge gathered through the physical senses and secular study, rather than through spiritual revelation.</note> is as impossible as *for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle*, or for a rib to regulate the movements of the purest fibres of the chest or of the heart;—so gross, yea, much more so, are the <term>sensual</term> <note>Refers to the lowest level of human thought, which is entirely dependent on the physical senses.</note> and scientific principles when compared with such as are spiritual and celestial. He who seeks only to investigate the secrets of nature, which are innumerable, with difficulty discovers a single one, and, as experience proves, in the course of his investigation, is liable to fall into many errors. How much more likely then is this to be the case, whilst investigating the hidden truths of spiritual and celestial life, where myriads of mysteries exist for one that is to be found in nature! 

For the sake of illustrating this point let us take the following instance: man of himself cannot act otherwise than wickedly, and avert himself from the Lord, yet it is not the man who acts thus, but as he is incited by the evil spirits who are attendant upon him; nor do the evil spirits so act except from the evil itself which they have appropriated; nevertheless man does evil and turns himself away from the Lord, and is in fault; and yet he lives only from the Lord. So, on the other hand, man of himself cannot possibly do good, and turn towards the Lord, but by the <term>ministry of angels</term> <note>The author posits that human thoughts and actions are influenced by a constant connection to the spiritual world through both heavenly and hellish beings.</note>; neither can the angels except from the Lord alone; and yet man may as of himself do good, and turn to the Lord. 

Neither the senses, nor science, nor philosophy, can conceive such truths as these, and, if consulted, would utterly deny their possibility although in themselves most certain; and so it is in all other similar cases. From what has been said it is evident that those who consult the senses and science respecting what is to be believed, not only precipitate themselves into doubt, but also into denial, and thus into darkness, and into every <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Intense worldly desires or selfish cravings that draw a person away from spiritual health.</note>. For such persons as believe what is false, act accordingly, and, denying the existence of what is spiritual and celestial, believe only what is corporeal and worldly. Thus they love whatever is of themselves and the world, and, a false sentiment removing all restraint over the inclinations of the natural man, gives rise to evils of life.

### THE CONTENTS.

234. The subsequent state of the <term>church</term> <note>In this context, the "church" refers to the collective spiritual state of humanity at that time.</note> down to the flood is here described; and as at that time the church utterly destroyed itself, it is foretold that the Lord would come into the world, and save the human race.
235. Being unwilling to believe any thing which could not be apprehended by the senses, the <term>sensual principle</term> <note>The level of thought entirely dependent on physical senses.</note>, which is *the serpent*, cursed itself, and became internal, verse 14.
236. To prevent therefore all mankind from falling into hell, the Lord promised that he would come into the world, verse 15.
237. The church is further exemplified by the woman, who so loved self, or the <term>proprium</term> <note>A technical term for the "self-hood" or the ego; the feeling that one's life and will are entirely one's own.</note>, as to be no longer capable of apprehending truth, although the <term>rational principle</term> <note>The capacity for logical reasoning.</note> had been conferred upon her to *rule over her*, verse 16.
238. The quality of the rational principle is then described as consenting to the suggestions of the *proprium*, and thus cursing itself, and becoming infernal, so that *reason* no longer remained, but <term>ratiocination</term> <note>Circular or false reasoning based only on outward appearances and self-interest.</note>, verse 17.
239. The curse and <term>vastation</term> <note>The process of being emptied of all spiritual truth and goodness.</note> are described, and also their <term>ferine</term> <note>Wild, savage, or animal-like.</note> nature, verse 18.
240. Also their aversion to every thing of faith and love; and thus from being man they became not men, verse 19.

### THE INTERNAL SENSE.

241. THE most ancient people, being <term>celestial men</term> <note>People whose primary motivation was love for the Divine, rather than mere intellectual understanding.</note>, were so constituted, that every object which they beheld, either in the world or upon the face of the earth, produced indeed the ordinary impression on their natural eye, but at the same time

excited in their minds a perception of the heavenly and divine realities which they signified and represented; their sight was thus only a kind of <term>instrumental sense</term> <note>A sense used as a tool to perceive higher truths, rather than an end in itself.</note>, and their language thence partook of a similar character. Every one, by consulting his own experience, may in some measure apprehend how this was; for whoever attends earnestly to the meaning of what is spoken by another, hears indeed the words which he employs, and yet as it were does not hear them, for he regards their sense only; and he who thinks still more deeply does not even attend to the mere meaning of the expressions used, but to the *universal* sense. These descendants, however, of whom the Word here treats, were unlike their forefathers; for in consequence of their love being placed on worldly and terrestrial objects, the sight of them induced a permanent impression on their minds; on these their thoughts were first employed, and, from the ideas thence acquired, they cogitated respecting celestial and divine things. 

Thus the <term>sensual principle</term> <note>The part of the human mind that focuses entirely on information from the five physical senses.</note> became with them the *principal*, instead of being esteemed, as by their ancestors, merely as the instrumental; and, whenever what is worldly and terrestrial is regarded as the principal, then men reason from those physical things on heavenly things, and thus bring on themselves spiritual blindness. Every one may comprehend this also from his own experience; for he must have remarked that whenever he does not attend to the sense of a speaker, but rather to his words, he carries away with him but little of their meaning, and knows almost nothing about their universal sense, because he is judging perhaps from a single word, or even from a single grammatical construction.

242. *And Jehovah God said to the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above every beast, and above every wild beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life.* Jehovah God's speaking to the serpent signifies that they perceived the sensual principle was the cause of their fall; and by the serpent's being cursed above every beast and every wild beast of the field, it is signified that the sensual principle averted itself from the celestial and turned towards the <term>corporeal</term> <note>Relating to the physical body and its base urges.</note>, and thus cursed itself. *The beast and the wild beast of the field* signify affections—feelings and desires—here as before; and the serpent's going on his belly signifies that the sensual principle could no longer look upwards towards celestial things, but downwards only towards such as are corporeal and terrestrial. *To eat dust all the days of its life* means that the sensual principle could no longer live except on what was corporeal and terrestrial, and thus had become <term>infernal</term> <note>Associated with a hellish or spiritually dead state.</note>.

243. In the most ancient celestial man, every thing belonging to the bodily senses being in order, yielded obedience and service to the <term>internal man</term> <note>The higher, spiritual part of the human mind that is open to heaven.</note>, and was no further regarded; but when men began to love themselves, and preferred sensual things—

245. *His saying to the serpent, Thou art cursed above every beast, and above every wild beast of the field*, signifies that the sensual principle averted itself from the celestial, turned towards the corporeal, and thereby condemned or cursed itself, as may be clearly demonstrated from the internal sense of the Word. <note>The "internal sense" refers to the hidden, spiritual meaning within the literal stories of the Bible.</note> Jehovah God, or the Lord, never curses any one; He is never angry with any one, never leads any into temptation, punishes none, and still less does he curse any. All this is, however, done by the infernal crew, for such actions can never proceed from the fountain of mercy, peace, and goodness. The reason of its being said, both here and in other parts of the Word, that Jehovah God not only turns away his face, is angry, punishes, and tempts, but also kills and even curses, is, that men may believe the Lord governs and disposes all and every thing in the universe, even evil itself, punishments, and temptations; and when they have received this most general idea, may afterwards learn how he governs and disposes all things by turning the evil of punishment and of temptation into good. In teaching and learning the Word, the most general truths must be first considered; such therefore abound in the literal sense.

246. *The beast and the wild beast of the field* signify <term>affections</term> <note>In this context, "affections" means the various loves, desires, or emotional states of the human heart.</note>, as is evident from what was previously said concerning them, (n. 45 and 46;) to which it is permitted to add the following passage from David: "Thou, O God, hast made to agitate the rain of benevolences, thou confirmest thy laboring inheritance: thy wild beast shall dwell therein," (Psalm lxviii. 9, 10;) where *also wild beast* denotes the affection of *good*, because it is said it shall *dwell in the inheritance of God*. 250\. Verse 15. *And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; He shall tread upon thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.* Every one is aware that this is the first prophecy of the Lord's advent into the world; it appears indeed clearly from the words themselves, and therefore from hence and from the prophets, even the Jews knew that a Messiah was about to come. Hitherto, however, no one has understood what is specifically meant by *the serpent, the woman, the serpent's seed, the woman's seed, the head of the serpent* which *was to be trodden upon, and the heel* which *the serpent should bruise*, they must therefore be explained. By *the serpent* is here meant every evil in general, and specifically *self-love*: by *the woman* is understood *the church*; by *the seed of the serpent*, all infidelity; by *the seed of the woman*, faith in the Lord; by *He*, the Lord himself; by *the head of the serpent*, the dominion of evil in general, and specifically of *self-love*; by *to tread upon*, depression, so that it should go *upon the belly and eat dust*; and by *the heel*, the lowest natural <term>principle</term> <note>In this context, a "principle" refers to a fundamental component or level of the human mind.</note>, as *the corporeal, which the serpent should bruise.*

Thus we read in Isaiah: "Rejoice not, thou whole Palestina, because the rod which smiteth thee is broken; for out of the *serpent's root* shall go forth a *cockatrice* [regulus], and his fruit shall be a *fiery flying serpent*." ### THE INTERNAL SENSE.

286. THIS and the preceding chapters, to the verses now under consideration, treat of the <term>most ancient people</term> <note>The author refers to the very first era of humanity, which he believes was in a state of perfect spiritual harmony before a gradual decline.</note>, and of their <term>regeneration</term> <note>The process of being spiritually reborn or made new by God.</note>: primarily, of those who had lived like wild beasts, but at length became spiritual men; then of those who became <term>celestial men</term> <note>People who act from a position of pure love and goodness, the highest spiritual state.</note>, and constituted the Most Ancient Church; afterwards of those who fell away and their descendants, detailed in regular order through the first, second, and third posterity and their successors, down to the deluge. In the verses following, which conclude the chapter, we have a recapitulation of what occurred from the period when the man of the Most Ancient Church was formed until the flood; thus it is a summary of all that has been previously stated.

287. Verse 20. *And the man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.* By man <note>original Latin: "homo" – referring to a human being or humanity in a general sense.</note> is here understood the man <note>original Latin: "vir" – referring specifically to a husband or the male aspect, often symbolizing the intellect or the person of the church.</note> of the Most Ancient Church, or the celestial man <note>original Latin: "homo"</note>, and by the wife and mother of all living, the church. She is called *mother*, as being the first church, and *living*, in consequence of possessing faith towards the Lord, who is life itself.

288. By *man* is denoted the man of the Most Ancient Church, or the celestial man, as was previously shown; and, at the same time, it was also demonstrated that the Lord alone is *man*, and that every celestial man derives his existence from him, because he is his likeness. Hence every member of the church, without distinction, was denominated a *man*, and at length this name was applied to all mankind, to distinguish them from the beasts.

289. It was also shown above that by *wife* is meant the church, and in a universal sense the kingdom of the Lord in the heavens and in the earths, and the same is understood by *mother*, as follows of consequence. In the Word <note>The author's term for the Sacred Scriptures or the Bible.</note> the church is very frequently called *mother*, as in Isaiah: "Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement?" **302.** The Jewish people were so inclined toward profanation that the secret truths of faith were never revealed to them. For this reason, it was never explicitly told to them that they would live after death, nor that the Lord would come into the world to save them. In fact, they were—and still are—kept in such ignorance and blindness that they have not known, and do not now know, of the existence of the internal man <note>The "internal man" refers to the spiritual part of a person that belongs to the soul and the afterlife, as opposed to the "external man" belonging to the physical world.</note>, or indeed of anything spiritual. If they had known these things, or if they acknowledged them now, their nature is such that they would treat them with contempt and violence. This would close off all hope of their salvation in the next life. This is what the Lord meant in the Gospel of John: “He has blinded their eyes and closed their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and turn themselves, and I should heal them” (John 12:40). This is also why the Lord spoke to them in parables without explaining their meaning; as He Himself said, “Seeing they should see, and hearing they should hear, and understand” (Matthew 13:13). For the same reason, all the deep truths of faith were hidden from them and concealed within the symbolic rituals of their Church, and the writings of the prophets were composed in a similar style. It is, however, one thing to know a truth, and another to truly accept it. A person who knows something but does not accept it is as if they never knew it at all; but the Lord is specifically referring to those who truly acknowledge a holy truth and afterwards speak against it or treat it with contempt.

**303.** A person’s life is shaped by the convictions they embrace—in other words, by what they truly acknowledge and believe. Something that a person is not convinced of, or does not acknowledge, cannot affect their mind. Therefore, it is impossible to treat something holy with profanation unless one has first believed and acknowledged that it is holy, only to later deny it. Those who may have information but do not truly believe it are like people who know nothing, or like those who deal with unimportant matters. This was the state of the Jewish people around the time of the Lord’s arrival. Regarding such people, the Lord says in Isaiah: “Go and tell this people: Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive. The expression *to live* is used with a similar signification by Ezekiel: "Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and make to live souls to you, and profane me with my people,—slaying the souls which should not *die*, and making the souls to *live* which should not *live*," (Ezekiel 13:18, 19.)

305. *Verse* 23. *Therefore Jehovah God sent him forth from the garden of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken.* *To be cast out of the garden of Eden* is to be deprived of all intelligence and wisdom, and *to till the ground from which he was taken* is to become **corporeal** <note>To become "corporeal" means to focus entirely on physical senses and worldly desires, losing connection to the spiritual or higher mind.</note>, as he was previous to **regeneration** <note>Regeneration is the process of being spiritually reborn or made new by turning away from selfish desires toward a life of love and faith.</note>.

To be cast out of the garden of Eden is to be deprived of all intelligence and wisdom, as is manifest from the signification of a *garden*, and of *Eden*, as given above; for a *garden* signifies intelligence, or the understanding of truth, and *Eden*, being significative of love, signifies wisdom, or the will of good.

To till the ground from which he was taken signifies to become corporeal, such as he was before regeneration, as was shown above (verse 19), where a similar expression occurs.

# GENESIS. [Chap. iii.

306. Verse 24. *And he drove out the man; and he made cherubim from the east to dwell at the garden of Eden, and the flame of a sword turning itself, to keep the way of the tree of lives.* To drive out the man is to deprive him entirely of all the will of good and understanding of truth, so that he is separated from them, and is no longer man. To make *cherubim* <note>Cherubim here are not just winged angels, but represent the Lord's "Providence"—the protective care that prevents people from accessing holy things they would only misuse or destroy.</note> from the east to dwell, is to provide against his entering into any mystery of faith; for the east to the *garden of Eden* is the celestial [principle] <note>The "celestial principle" refers to the highest state of love and goodness in the human heart.</note> from which is intelligence, and by *cherubim*, the Providence of the Lord is signified, preventing such a man from entering into the things of faith. By the *flame of a sword turning itself*, is signified self-love with its unruly desires and consequent persuasions, which are such that he wishes, indeed, to enter, but is carried away thence to corporeal and terrestrial things, and this for the purpose of *keeping the way of the tree of lives* <note>While usually called the "Tree of Life," the original Hebrew uses the plural "lives" to signify both the spiritual life of the heart and the intellectual life of the mind.</note>, that is, to prevent the profanation of holy things.

307. It here treats of the sixth and seventh posterity, which perished by the flood, and were altogether cast out of the *garden of Eden*, or from all understanding of truth, and thus ceasing, as it were, to be *men*, they were left to their insane lusts and persuasions.

308. As the signification of the *east* and of the *garden of Eden* were given above, it is needless to dwell longer on them; but that *cherubim* denote the Providence of the Lord, lest man should insanely enter upon the mysteries of faith, from the <term>proprium</term> <note>original: "proprium." This term refers to the human "selfhood" or ego—the sense that one's life, thoughts, and abilities belong to oneself rather than being a gift from the Divine.</note> and the <term>sensual and scientific [principle]</term> <note>original: "sensuali et scientifico." These terms refer to knowledge gained exclusively through the five senses and worldly study, rather than through spiritual insight.</note>, and thus profane them, and destroy himself, is demonstrated by all the passages in the Word where mention is made of *cherubim*. As the Jews were of such a quality, that if they had possessed any clear knowledge concerning the Lord's coming,—the representatives or types of the church significative of Him—the life after death,—the interior man and the internal sense of the Word, they would have profaned it, and have perished eternally; therefore this was represented by the *cherubim* on the mercy-seat over the ark, over the curtains of the tabernacle, over the vail, and also in the temple, and it signified that the Lord had them in keeping, (Exod. xxv. 18—21; xxvi. 1, 31; 1 Kings vi. 23—29, 32.) For the ark, in which was the testimony, signified the same as the *tree of lives* in this passage, that is, the Lord and celestial things, which belong solely to Him. Hence also the Lord is so often called the God of Israel sitting upon the *cherubim*, and hence he spake with Moses and Aaron between the *cherubim*, (Exod. xxv. 22; Numb. vii. 89.) This is plainly described in Ezekiel, where it is said, "The glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the *cherub* whereupon he was, to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed with linen,—and—said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon

The mind consists of two parts, the **will** and the **understanding**. Love or good belongs to the will, faith or the true to the understanding; and from love or good that people perceived every thing relating to faith or truth, and thus their mind was single, or a one. With the posterity of such a race, seed of the same celestial origin necessarily remains, so that any falling away from truth and good on their part is attended with the most dangerous consequences, since their whole mind becomes so perverted as to render a restoration scarcely possible in another life. It is otherwise with those who do not possess celestial but only spiritual seed, as the people after the deluge, and also the present generation of mankind. There is no love in them, consequently no will to goodness, but still there is a capacity of receiving faith, or the understanding of the true, by means of which some degree of charity can be induced, although by a different process, namely, by the insinuation of conscience from the Lord grounded in the knowledges of truth and its derivative goodness. These are <term>arcana</term><note>Latin for "secrets" or "mysteries"; here referring to hidden spiritual truths.</note> with which the present generation of mankind are utterly unacquainted, since in modern times none understand the nature of the celestial man, nor even that of the spiritual man, still less the quality of the human mind and life thence resulting, and the consequent state after death.

311. The condition of those who perished by the flood is such in the other life, that they cannot exist anywhere in the **world of spirits** <note>An intermediate state between heaven and hell where souls are prepared for their final destination.</note>, or with other spirits, but are in a hell separated from the hells of others, and as it were under a certain mountain. This appears as an intermediate mountain in consequence of their direful phantasies and persuasions. Their phantasies and persuasions are such as to produce so profound a stupor in other spirits that they do not know whether they are alive or dead, for they deprive them of all understanding of truth, so that they can perceive nothing. Such also was their persuasion during their abode in the world; and because it was foreseen that in another life they would be incapable of associating with other spirits, without occasioning in them an appearance of death, they were all destroyed, and the Lord of his divine mercy induced other states on those who lived after the deluge.

313. From what is here stated of the first man, it is manifest that all hereditary evil existing in the present day was not derived from him, as is commonly, but falsely supposed. Every attentive observer may see evidence of this truth in the fact, that the evil inclinations of parents remain visibly in their children, so that a family, yea, an entire race, may be thereby distinguished from every other.

316. *When the soul thus separates himself, he is received by good spirits, who likewise do him all kind offices whilst he is in consort with them. If, however, his life in the world was such that he cannot remain associated with the good, he seeks to be disunited from them also, and this separation is repeated again and again, until he associates himself with those whose state entirely agrees with that of his former life in the world, among whom he finds, as it were, his own life. 317. *Some are, however, conveyed more slowly, and others more speedily, to heaven; indeed I have seen those who were elevated to heaven immediately after death, of which I am permitted here to mention only two instances.*

318. *A certain [spirit] came and discoursed with me, who, it was evident from some appearances about him, had only lately died. At first he knew not where he was, supposing himself still to be in the world; but when he became conscious of having entered upon another mode of existence, and that he no longer possessed anything—as house, wealth, and the like—being in another kingdom, where he was deprived of all he had in the world, he was seized with anxiety, and knew not where to betake himself, or whither to go for a place of abode. He was then informed that the Lord alone provides for him and for all; and was left to himself, that his thoughts might take their wonted direction, as in the world. He now considered (for in another life the thoughts of all may be plainly perceived) what he must do, being deprived of all means of subsistence; and whilst in this state of anxiety, he was brought into association with some celestial spirits, who belonged to the province of the heart* <note>In this spiritual anatomy, different groups of angels correspond to different organs of the human body; the "province of the heart" represents those who are grounded in the highest form of love.</note>, *and who showed him every attention which he could desire. This being done, he was again left to himself, and beginning to consider, from a principle of charity* <note>original: "charitas." Here meaning active, selfless love for others rather than just financial almsgiving.</note>, *how he might repay so great kindness, it was evident from this, that whilst he had lived in the body he was principled in charity grounded in faith, and he was therefore immediately taken up into heaven.*

319. *I have also seen another person immediately translated into heaven by the angels, who was accepted by the Lord, and shown the glory of heaven; not to mention much other experience respecting some who had to wait their periods of probation* <term>probation</term><note>A period of testing or adjustment after death where a spirit's true inner nature is revealed before they transition to their permanent spiritual home.</note>.

## CHAPTER FOUR

->ON THE NATURE OF THE LIFE OF THE SOUL OR SPIRIT<-

**320. WITH** *respect to the general circumstances relating to the mode of life of souls, or newly arrived spirits <note>The original term is "novitiate spirits," referring to those who have recently passed from the physical world into the spiritual realm.</note> after death, it was demonstrated to me on numerous occasions that when a person enters upon eternal life, they are initially unaware of it. They imagine themselves still to be in the world, and indeed, still within their own body. Consequently, upon being informed that they are now a spirit, they are filled with wonder and astonishment. This is both because they find themselves exactly like a human being in terms of their senses, desires, and thoughts, and because they did not believe, during their life in the world, that the spirit was a real entity—or, as is the case with some, they did not believe a spirit could possess the tangible form they now experience.*

**321.** *Another circumstance to be noted is that a spirit enjoys much more excellent sensory faculties, and far superior powers of thinking and speaking, than when they were living in the physical body. In fact, the former earthly state can scarcely be compared with this new state, although spirits are not aware of this until the Lord grants them the opportunity to reflect upon it.*

**322.** *Care should be taken not to give credit to the erroneous opinion that spirits do not possess far more exquisite <note>In this context, "exquisite" means highly refined, intense, or acute.</note> sensations than they did during their life in the body; I have been convinced of the contrary by experience repeated thousands of times. Should anyone be unwilling to believe this fact due to their preconceived ideas about the nature of the spirit, let them see for themselves when they enter the next life, where they will be compelled to believe by their own direct experience. Spirits not only possess the faculty of sight, but they live in a light to which the mid-day light of our world cannot be compared. This is especially true for good spirits, angelic spirits, and angels. Regarding the nature of the light in which they dwell and by which they see, we shall—by the divine mercy of the Lord <note>original: "ex Divina Domini misericordia"; a recurring phrase emphasizing that all spiritual revelation is considered a gift from God.</note>—treat on that subject later. They also enjoy the power of hearing, and to such an acute degree that it vastly exceeds what they possessed in the body. I have been convinced of this through almost constant conversations with them for several years now. The nature of their speech, as well as the sense of smell they possess, will also be considered hereafter. Furthermore, they possess a most acute sense of <term>touch</term> <note>The author posits that all senses—sight, hearing, etc.—are actually specialized variations of touch, meaning the spirit's "feeling" of reality is much more direct.</note>, which is the source of the pains and torments endured in hell; for all sensations are related to touch, being merely diversities and varieties of it. Their desires and affections, moreover, are incomparably stronger than those possessed during their earthly life; but more will be said on this subject*

## THE CONTENTS.

324. The Word <note>In this context, "The Word" refers to the Sacred Scripture or the Bible.</note> here treats of doctrines separate from the Church, or heresies, and of a new Church afterwards raised up, called *Enos*.

325. The <term>Most Ancient Church<note>This term refers to the symbolic first state of humanity—often associated with Adam—characterized by a direct, heart-centered connection to the Divine.</note></term> possessed faith in the Lord through the medium of love; but there were some who separated faith from love. The doctrine of faith separated from love was called *Cain*, and charity, which is love towards the neighbor, *Abel*, verses 1, 2.

326. The worship of each is described, that of faith separate from charity by the *offering of Cain*, and that of charity by the *offering of Abel*, verses 3, 4. That worship proceeding from charity was acceptable, but not worship originating in faith alone, is shown verses 4, 5.

327. The state of those who were principled in <term>faith alone<note>A theological concept where belief is considered sufficient for salvation, independent of one's actions or moral life (charity).</note></term> became evil, is described by *Cain’s anger being kindled, and his countenance falling*, verses 5, 6.

328. That the quality of faith is known by charity; and that charity wishes to abide with faith, if faith does not assume the pre-eminence, and exalt itself above charity, verse 7.

329. That charity is extinguished with such as have separated faith, and preferred it to charity, is described by *Cain's slaying his brother Abel*, verses 8, 9.

330. Charity extinguished is called *the voice of bloods* <note>original: "sanguinum." In the original Hebrew and Latin, "blood" is plural here, suggesting total violence or the destruction of all things good and true.</note>, verse 10; *perverse doctrine, the curse from the ground*, verse 11. The false and the evil originating thence are the *fugitive and vagabond in the earth*, verse 12. And as they averted themselves from the Lord, that they were in danger of *eternal death*, verses 13, 14. But, because by means of faith, charity was afterwards to be implanted, it was made inviolable; and this is signified by *the mark set upon Cain*, verse 15. And its removal from its former situation is denoted by *Cain's dwelling towards the east of Eden*, verse 16.

331. The amplification of that heresy is called *Enoch*, verse 17.

332. The heresies thence originating, each by its respective name, in the last of which, denominated *Lamech*, there was nothing of faith remaining, verse 18.

333. A new church then arose, which is understood by *Adah and Zillah*, and described by their sons *Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-Cain*. The <term>celestial<note>Relating to the highest love or the will.</note></term> things of the church were represented by *Jabal*, the <term>spiritual<note>Relating to truth or the intellect.</note></term> by *Jubal*, and the <term>natural<note>Relating to external life and physical skills.</note></term> by *Tubal-Cain*, verses 19—22.

334. The origin of that church, when every thing of faith and charity was extinguished, and violence done to what was most sacred, is described, verses 23, 24.

335. A general recapitulation of the subject is given ; after faith, signified by *Cain*, was separated from charity, a new faith...

## THE INTERNAL SENSE.
<note>The "Internal Sense" refers to the deeper, symbolic meaning of the Bible that relates to the human soul and spiritual life, as opposed to the literal historical narrative.</note>

337. SINCE this chapter treats of the degeneracy of the Most Ancient Church <note>This term refers to the symbolic first state of humanity, characterized by a direct, heart-centered connection to the Divine.</note>, or the falsification of its doctrine, and consequently of heresies and sects, under the names of Cain and his descendants, it is to be observed, that there is no possibility of understanding how doctrine was falsified, or what was the nature of the heresies and sects of that church, unless the nature of the true church be rightly understood. Enough has been said above concerning the Most Ancient Church, showing that it was a <term>celestial man<note>A "celestial man" is one who acts from love and feeling rather than just from intellectual knowledge or rules.</note></term>, and acknowledged no other faith than such as was connected with love towards the Lord and the neighbor. By means of that love from the Lord, they obtained faith, or a perception of all its truths, and were therefore unwilling to speak of faith, lest it should be separated from love, as was shown above (n. 200, 203). Such is the nature of the celestial man, and in this character he is described by David by representatives, where the Lord is spoken of as the *King*, and the celestial man as the *King’s son*:

> “Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness to the king’s son.—The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the hills, by righteousness. They shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure throughout all generations. In his days shall the righteous flourish, and abundance of peace, until there be no moon,” (Psalm 72:1, 3, 5, 7.)

By the *sun*, love is signified; by the *moon*, faith; by <term>mountains and hills<note>In the symbolic language of the Bible, mountains often represent the highest types of love, while hills represent slightly lower, but still spiritual, affections.</note></term>, the Most Ancient Church; by *throughout all generations*, the churches after the flood; *until there be no moon*, denotes that faith will become love:—see also what is said in Isaiah 30:26. Such was the nature of the Most Ancient Church and of its doctrine; but the case is far different at the present day, for now faith precedes charity, and by means of faith, charity is given by the Lord, and then charity takes the precedence. It hence follows, that doctrine became falsified in ancient times when men made confession of faith, and thus separated it from love. Those who falsified doctrine in this way, or separated faith from love, or acknowledged faith alone, were there denominated *Cain*; and this thing was regarded by them as an enormous [*heresy*].

338. Verse 1. *And the man knew Eve his wife, and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man*, Jehovah.

It contrasts the "Most Ancient Church," which prioritized love, with later states where faith and knowledge became primary.</summary>

-># GENESIS. [CHAP. IV]<-

By the *man* and his *wife* the <term>Most Ancient Church<note>A symbolic term for the first era of humanity, which the author describes as being in a state of pure love and direct connection with the Divine.</note></term> is signified as has been shown above: its first offspring, or first-born, is faith which is here called *Cain*; the saying, *I have gotten a man, Jehovah*, signifies that faith with such as are called *Cain*, is known and acknowledged in a distinct form.

339. In the three foregoing chapters it was so abundantly shown, that by the *man* and his *wife* the <term>Most Ancient Church</term> is signified, that on this point there can remain no doubt; and this being admitted, it is evident that the conception and offspring of that Church can be no other than we have stated. It was customary with the most ancient people to give names, by which they represented events, and thus framed a genealogy; for whatever has relation to the church may be considered in this light, since one faith is conceived and born of another, like an ordinary generation. Hence it is common in the Word <note>The "Word" is a term used by the author to refer to the Sacred Scriptures or the Bible.</note> to name various circumstances relating to the church, *conceptions*, *births*, *offspring*, *infants*, *little children*, *sons*, *daughters*, *young men*, &c.; the prophetical parts of the Word abound with such expressions.

340. That the saying *I have gotten a man, Jehovah*, signifies that faith, with such as are called *Cain*, is known and acknowledged as a thing by itself, is evident from what was said in the introduction to this chapter. They had been, as it were, previously, ignorant of faith as a separate object of thought, because they had a perception <note>"Perception" here refers to an intuitive, internal "knowing" of what is true and good, which the author believes preceded the need for written laws or doctrines.</note> of whatever related to it; but, when they began to make a distinct doctrine of faith, they then collected together the truths which they had perceived, and reduced them into doctrine, calling it *I have gotten a man, Jehovah*, as if they had found out somewhat new; and thus, what was before inscribed on the heart became a mere matter of science <note>The author uses "science" in the older sense of "knowledge" or "information"—meaning they moved from feeling the truth to merely knowing it as a set of facts.</note>. In ancient times they gave every new thing a name, and explained what the name implied by particular sayings. Thus the signification of the name <term>Ishmael</term> is explained by the saying, "*Jehovah hath heard his affliction*," (Gen. xvi. 11;) that of <term>Reuben</term>, by the expression, "*Jehovah hath looked upon thy affliction*," (Gen. xxix. 32;) the name <term>Simeon</term>, by the saying, "*Jehovah hath heard that I was hated*," (Gen. xxix. 33;) and that of <term>Judah</term> by, "*Now will I praise Jehovah*," (verse 35.) The altar built by <term>Moses</term> was called, "*Jehovah my banner*." (Exodus xvii. 15;) and in like manner the doctrine of faith is here denominated "*I have gotten a man, Jehovah*," or *Cain*.

341. Verse 2. *And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a shepherd of the flock, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.* The second offspring of the church is <term>charity<note>In this context, "charity" means more than just giving to the poor; it signifies a spiritual love for others and the active practice of doing good.</note></term>, signified by the terms *Abel* and brother. He is a *shepherd of the flock* who exercises the good of <term>charity</term>, and a *tiller of the ground* is one who is destitute of <term>charity</term>, although principled in faith separate from love, which is, indeed, no faith.
